title: When Will the AI Bubble Burst? Watch Credit Default Swaps and Token Prices
dek: The AI bubble will eventually burst, but current valuations are far below dot-com levels — Nvidia trades at just 15x earnings. The real risk lies in credit markets, where credit default swaps have risen to historic highs, signalling a possible sharp correction ahead.
why: Dan Niles offers quantitative indicators for judging the AI bubble (token prices, cloud vendor margins) and a distinctive lens (credit markets, Chinese semiconductors) that has practical reference value for understanding the current market phase.
who: Fund managers watching the AI investment cycle, tech stock investors, and founders who want to understand the risks and opportunities of the AI bubble.
skip: The opening small talk and the closing section about gaming can be skipped; the core content starts at the 4-minute mark.

points.h: Token prices fell 50% but volume rose 2.5x
points.body: Dan Niles points out that to judge whether the AI bubble has peaked, you need to watch two core variables: token output and unit price. Since the end of May, due to competition from open-source models, the unit price of tokens has fallen about 50%, but output over the same period has grown 2.5x. As long as volume growth offsets the price decline, industry revenue is still expanding. Meanwhile, revenue growth at the three major cloud vendors (AWS, Azure, GCP) accelerated from 35% in March to 43% in June, with operating margins up about 2 percentage points, showing the industry's fundamentals remain healthy.

points.h: 4x leverage was the main cause of the fund's blow-up
points.body: The Situational Awareness fund's blow-up was not because its positions were directionally wrong, but because it used 4x leverage. If the underlying falls 25%, 4x leverage means a 100% loss, triggering liquidation. This resembles the lesson of Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) in 1998. After hearing about the fund's problems on July 29, Dan Niles judged that a short-term bottom was near, because the fundamentals (token usage growth) had not deteriorated. He warns that leverage amplifies risk in both directions, and especially when long and short positions are both unfavourable, it can trigger catastrophic selling.

points.h: Cloud vendors' cash flow turned negative for the first time
points.body: Although cloud vendors' revenue is accelerating and margins are improving, the market is worried about their deteriorating free cash flow. For example, Google's cash flow turned negative for the first time since its IPO, due to massive AI capex. Dan Niles believes this resembles the dot-com era: the technological revolution was real, but stocks could still plunge 78% (Nasdaq 2000-2002). He expects strong industry growth over the next year, but once a hyperscaler cuts capex due to debt problems, it could trigger a chain reaction.

points.h: Data centre political risk is the biggest short-term threat
points.body: Dan Niles points out that the biggest short-term risk to AI growth is not demand, but political resistance. A Gallup poll shows 71% of people oppose a data centre in their own backyard, higher than the 53% who oppose a nuclear power plant. Both parties rarely agree on anything, but they agree on opposing data centres, especially in red states like Texas. Hyperscalers have failed to effectively publicise the jobs and tax revenue data centres bring, while anti-business forces have successfully painted them as a negative. He expects political risk to weigh on the market before the November midterm elections.

points.h: Chinese semiconductors will break the cyclicality myth
points.body: Dan Niles believes the view that semiconductors are no longer cyclical is dangerous, and China could be the key to breaking that myth. He draws an analogy to Japan in the 1980s and South Korea in the 1990s entering the DRAM market with government support, eventually displacing US dominance. Today, China's CXMT (ChangXin Memory Technologies) and YMTC (Yangtze Memory Technologies) are expanding rapidly. CXMT plans to raise monthly capacity from 300,000 wafers to 500,000, and YMTC aims to surpass Samsung and SK Hynix in NAND. For China, semiconductor self-sufficiency matters more than aircraft carriers.

points.h: Agentic AI will extend the cycle by at least a year
points.body: Dan Niles believes agentic AI is a brand-new phase, marked by the launch of the OpenClaw project on January 30 this year. The agentic phase consumes 10-100x more tokens than chat AI, which will drive continued demand growth. He expects the stock market to have at least another year of upside, but warns to watch out for competition such as Chinese memory chips. He reminds investors to watch the data like a hawk and avoid excessive optimism or pessimism.

points.h: Software faces AI disruption; security and gaming are relatively safe
points.body: Dan Niles believes AI's impact on software is enormous. OpenAI and Anthropic's combined annualised revenue soared from $29 billion at the start of the year to $105 billion seven months later, and that spending must squeeze other software budgets. He favours three relatively safe areas: cybersecurity, recording systems, and video games. Recent news — Salesforce partnering with Anthropic, Workday being acquired by Silver Lake — suggests software stocks may be near a bottom, but security sector valuations are already high.

points.h: Credit markets are the AI bubble's early warning system
points.body: Dan Niles stresses that credit markets are key to judging the AI bubble. He monitors daily the credit default swap (CDS) prices of hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Google, and Nvidia, and finds they are already above the North American investment-grade average and at historic highs. Credit investors are more cautious than equity investors because bond returns are fixed and principal safety must be ensured. AI's massive capex relies on debt financing, and 30-year Treasury yields have risen to their highest since 2007, increasing financing costs and potentially becoming the trigger for the bubble to burst.

quotes.text: There is a number of tokens produced and how much you can charge for each of those tokens. And what you've seen since the end of May is what you can charge for these tokens has gone down by about 50%.

The problem was that they were using 4x leverage. So, if you do the math and say: if you have a drawdown of 25 percent, but a leverage of 4 times, then you lose 100%, and at that point your fund is liquidated.
71% were against data centers and only 53% were against nuclear power. That's bad, right? I couldn't believe it when I saw it.

I think many investors greatly underestimate what China is doing. And I hear these arguments and I tell myself that this is exactly what people were thinking back in the 1980s when Japan entered the semiconductor industry.
The agent phase uses 10-100 times more tokens than the chat-based AI phase. So, I think you still have a long way to go, at least another year for the stock to go up.

When you have some of the largest companies in the world that generate the largest cash flow that have credit default swaps trading at premiums to North American investment-grade credit default swaps, that tells you about the ability of the capital markets to absorb that.
